title: By Faith: The Great Cloud of Witnesses
summary: Faith is the assurance of what is hoped for and the certainty of what is not seen. The author traces it through the history of God's people: Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham and Sarah, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, the Israelites at the Red Sea and Jericho, and Rahab, then a rush of judges, kings, prophets, and unnamed sufferers. All of them trusted God's promise without receiving its fulfillment in their lifetime, because God planned something better, so that only together with us would they be made perfect.
story: Chapter 10 ended with Habakkuk's words, "My righteous one will live by faith", and with the author's confidence that his readers are among those who have faith and preserve their souls. Chapter 11 shows what that faith looks like by walking through the Old Testament story from creation to the Maccabean martyrs. It is a history of Israel told as a history of trust. The chapter prepares for chapter 12, where the witnesses surround the readers like a crowd in a stadium, and Jesus himself is presented as the founder and perfecter of faith.
historical:
The examples come in rough chronological order. Verses 3-7 draw on Genesis 1-9: creation, Abel's sacrifice (Genesis 4), Enoch taken by God (Genesis 5:24), and Noah's ark (Genesis 6-9). Verses 8-22 cover the patriarchs in Genesis 12-50, including Abraham's call, Sarah's conception of Isaac, the binding of Isaac (Genesis 22), and Joseph's instructions about his bones (Genesis 50:24-25). Verses 23-31 follow Moses and the exodus through the fall of Jericho and the rescue of Rahab (Exodus 2-14, Joshua 2 and 6). Verse 32 names judges and kings from Judges and Samuel, not in chronological order (Barak came before Gideon, and Jephthah before Samson).

Verses 33-38 allude to many stories without names. Shutting the mouths of lions recalls Daniel (Daniel 6); quenching fire recalls his three friends (Daniel 3); women receiving back their dead recalls the widow of Zarephath and the Shunammite woman (1 Kings 17, 2 Kings 4). Those who were tortured and refused release to gain a better resurrection most likely refers to the martyrs under the Seleucid king Antiochus IV around 167 BC, whose stories are told in 2 Maccabees 6-7. Being sawed in two probably refers to a Jewish tradition that the prophet Isaiah was martyred this way under King Manasseh, a tradition found in a later writing called the Martyrdom of Isaiah. Hebrews draws freely on the whole memory of Israel, not only the books of the Hebrew Bible.
cultural:
Lists of heroes were a familiar form in Jewish and Greek writing. The Jewish wisdom book Sirach (chapters 44-50) praises Israel's famous ancestors in order, and 1 Maccabees 2:51-60 records a dying father reminding his sons of the deeds of the ancestors to strengthen them for battle. Greek and Roman writers used similar lists of examples to teach virtue. Hebrews adapts the form, but with a difference: the heroes are praised not for courage or wisdom as such but for faith in God's promise, and many of them are remembered for what they suffered rather than what they achieved.

The language of strangers and exiles (verse 13) described resident foreigners who lived in a place without citizenship and could be treated with suspicion. Abraham lived in tents in the land he was promised, never owning it except for a burial plot (Genesis 23). The author presents this status as the normal condition of faith: God's people do not belong fully to any earthly city because they are seeking the city God has prepared.
literary: The chapter is built on the repeated phrase "By faith" (one word in Greek, pistei), a device called anaphora, which gives it the rhythm of a litany. After the opening definition (verses 1-2) the author moves through creation and the primeval figures (verses 3-7), Abraham and the patriarchs (verses 8-22), Moses and the exodus generation (verses 23-31), and a rapid, breathless summary (verses 32-38) that begins with the rhetorical "what more shall I say?" Twice the author pauses to comment. Verses 13-16 note that these people died without receiving the promise and were seeking a better, heavenly country. Verses 39-40 conclude the chapter with the same point: they were commended but did not receive what was promised, for God had something better in view. The chapter's structure moves from triumph (conquered kingdoms) to suffering (sawed in two), showing that faith is not measured by visible success.

outline.t: Abraham and Sarah: going out and receiving life
Isaac offered, and the patriarchs' blessings
Moses, the exodus, Jericho, and Rahab

doctrines.note: Faith in Hebrews is trust in God's promises when their fulfillment is still unseen. It is not a leap in the dark but confidence in the character of the God who promised: anyone who approaches him "must believe that He exists and that He rewards those who earnestly seek Him" (verse 6).
The heroes of faith looked forward: to a city with foundations, to a better country, to a better resurrection. Faith and hope are bound together, and both point beyond this life.

The list does not end with victories but with the tortured, imprisoned, and destitute, of whom "The world was not worthy". Faith can mean deliverance, but it can also mean enduring loss without deliverance in this life.
Faith begins with understanding that the universe was formed at God's command (verse 3). The visible world rests on the word of an invisible God.

words.note: Hupostasis, translated assurance in verse 1. It literally means what stands under, a foundation or underlying reality, and in 1:3 it described God's very being. Interpreters debate whether here it means the subjective confidence of the believer or the objective reality that faith grasps. Many see both: faith gives substance now to the things hoped for.

Elegchos, proof, evidence, or conviction, a word used of the argument that establishes a case. Faith is the certainty (the BSB's rendering) of what is not seen. It is not wishful thinking but a settled conviction grounded in God's word.

Parepidemos, a temporary resident, sojourner, or exile. The patriarchs acknowledged they were strangers and exiles on the earth (verse 13), and 1 Peter uses the same word for Christians scattered through Asia Minor. It describes a people whose true home lies ahead.

Pistis, faith, trust, or faithfulness, used twenty-four times in this chapter. In Greek the word can mean both believing and being trustworthy, and in Hebrews faith is always active: it obeys, goes out, offers, refuses, endures.

christ: The chapter shows the faith of those who lived before Christ, and Hebrews presents them as looking forward to what God would do. Moses "valued disgrace for Christ above the treasures of Egypt" (verse 26), an interpretation that sees his solidarity with God's suffering people as sharing in the reproach the Messiah would bear. Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead, and received Isaac back as a kind of foreshadowing, a pattern Christians have long connected with the resurrection. Most important, all these witnesses "did not receive what was promised" because the fulfillment comes through Christ. The chapter points directly to 12:2, where Jesus is the founder and perfecter of faith, the one in whom every promise reaches its goal and in whom the faithful of every age are made perfect together.

hard.q: Why are morally troubling figures like Samson, Jephthah, and Rahab held up as examples of faith?
hard.a:
Several people in the list have deeply troubling stories. Samson was reckless and violent, Jephthah made a rash vow that, on the most common reading, cost his daughter her life (Judges 11), Rahab was a prostitute who lied to protect the spies, and even Abraham, Jacob, and David had serious failures. The author does not commend all they did. He commends their faith: at a decisive moment each trusted God's promise and acted on it. Rahab welcomed the spies because she believed Israel's God was the true God (Joshua 2:9-11). Samson's last act was a prayer (Judges 16:28).

Interpreters also note that Hebrews selects examples from Scripture as it stands, and the Old Testament itself often narrates these figures' failures without comment, leaving readers to judge. The list shows that God works through flawed people who trust him, not through people who earn his favor. That is good news for the readers, who were failing too, but it is not an endorsement of every act of those named. The book of Judges itself presents its heroes as signs of Israel's decline, and Hebrews' list does not erase that verdict.

questions: Faith is described as certainty about what we do not see. What unseen realities shape the way you live, and how firmly do you hold them?
Many in this chapter died without receiving what was promised. How do you keep trusting God when the fulfillment of his promises seems far away?
The list includes flawed and even disreputable people. What does that say about who God can use and about how he sees you?
